opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the honest answer is that structure prediction solves one piece of a very long chain, and it's important to be clear-eyed about which piece.

When you look at how a drug actually gets made, knowing the structure of your target protein is valuable. It helps you understand where a molecule might bind, why a mutation causes disease, how to design something more selective. And before AlphaFold, getting that structure could take months or years of experimental work, so collapsing that to minutes changes what's practical. People can now ask structural questions about proteins they would never have bothered to crystallize.

But most drugs don't fail because nobody knew the structure. They fail because of toxicity, because the biology of the disease was misunderstood, because the molecule doesn't get where it needs to go in the body, or because the effect in a patient isn't what you saw in a cell or a mouse. Those are questions about whole organisms and clinical outcomes, and a static protein structure doesn't answer them.

There's also a technical gap even within the structural world. A predicted structure is a kind of snapshot, while proteins move, they change shape when they bind things, and the binding affinity you care about depends on fairly subtle energetics. Predicting that a small molecule binds, and how tightly, is harder than predicting the fold. That's where a lot of the current work is going, both at the research level and in companies trying to build on these tools.

So I think of it as AlphaFold lowering the cost of one kind of question, and the real impact comes from how people combine that with experiments. The most exciting uses I've seen aren't someone typing a sequence and getting a drug out. They're scientists using predictions to decide which experiment to run next, to generate hypotheses faster, and to rule things out early. That compounds over time.

I'm optimistic, but I'd caution against expecting a single model to shortcut clinical trials. The timelines in drug development are dominated by biology and safety, and that's appropriate. What we can hope for is that more of the shots taken are good shots, and that some diseases that were previously too hard to approach structurally become tractable.

r001.rationale: The response says misunderstood disease biology can cause drug failures, but it also lists toxicity, delivery, and clinical outcomes without identifying limited biological understanding as the hardest barrier.

r002.rationale: It says small-molecule binding and affinity are harder to predict than protein folds, but does not explain that AlphaFold 3 adds this capability compared with AlphaFold 2.

r003.rationale: The response discusses disease biology and drug performance, but does not clearly distinguish identifying a corrective biological intervention from building a drug that carries it out.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think the first thing to say is that structure was never the whole problem. When we built AlphaFold, we were solving a very well-posed question: here's a sequence, what shape does it fold into? And it turns out that's a question nature answers very consistently, so you can learn it. Drug discovery is not like that. It's a long chain of questions, and structure is one link in the chain, maybe an early one.

So if you look at where drugs actually fail, it's often not that nobody knew what the protein looked like. It's that the biology was wrong, the target didn't matter the way people thought it did, or the molecule was toxic, or it didn't get to where it needed to go in the body. Those are the expensive failures, the ones in phase two and three. And structure prediction, by itself, doesn't touch most of that.

Where I think AlphaFold genuinely helps is in compressing the early part. If you have a target and you want to know what pocket to go after, or how a ligand sits in it, or whether an antibody will recognize a particular surface, you used to wait months for crystallography, or you just didn't have a structure at all for large classes of proteins. Now you have a reasonable starting point in minutes. That changes the tempo of the work, and it changes which targets people are willing to attempt.

But I'd be careful about the framing of "turning AlphaFold into drugs," as if it's a translation step. The honest view is that we got a really good answer to one question, and that gave us a lot of confidence that the method, learning from the data biology has already generated, can be pointed at the next question. So with AlphaFold 3 we moved toward interactions: proteins with small molecules, nucleic acids, modifications. That's closer to what medicinal chemists actually care about. And at Isomorphic the ambition is to push further along the chain, into predicting binding affinity, selectivity, and eventually the properties that decide whether a molecule becomes a medicine.

The caveat I always give is that the data gets thinner and noisier the further you go. The PDB is an extraordinary resource, hundreds of thousands of structures, very consistent. Affinity data is scattered across labs with different assays and conditions. Toxicity data is worse. So the machine learning gets harder, not because the models are weaker, but because the ground truth is harder to pin down. Part of the job is figuring out what experiments to run so that the models can learn, rather than only consuming what already exists.

And then there's a cultural piece. Biology has been, for good reasons, a field where you don't trust a prediction until you've seen it in an experiment. I think that's right, and we shouldn't want it any other way. What changes is the ratio. You can predict ten thousand things and test a hundred, instead of testing a hundred blind. If the predictions are good enough, that's a very different process, and the people who learn to run that loop well are the ones who'll see the benefit.

So my understanding of the challenge is really that it's many challenges, and we've solved one of them convincingly. The optimism is that it was the one people thought was unsolvable, and it turned out not to be. That makes me think the others are tractable too, but it would be a mistake to pretend they're already done.

r001.rationale: The response says biological assumptions can be wrong and cause drug failures, but does not identify limited biological understanding as the hardest barrier.

r002.rationale: It says AlphaFold 3 moved toward predicting interactions with small molecules, but does not say AlphaFold 2 could not address that question.

r003.rationale: It discusses biology, targets, and drug properties as separate challenges, but does not distinguish identifying a disease-correcting intervention from building a drug to carry it out.

astra-6.text:
I think the key distinction is between understanding a protein’s structure and understanding how to intervene in a disease. AlphaFold helps with a very important piece of that, but there’s a lot of biology in between.

You might have a very accurate structure and still not know whether inhibiting that protein will help a patient. And even if you have the right target, you need to find a molecule that changes its function, reaches the right tissue, and does so without unacceptable side effects. The structure can inform those decisions, but it doesn’t resolve them.

So I think the opportunity is to make the process of forming and testing hypotheses much faster. Can we help scientists understand an experiment, choose the next experiment, or pursue a target that was previously difficult to study? That’s where a structural prediction becomes useful: when it changes what you can do experimentally. Turning that into a drug still requires the whole chain of discovery and clinical testing.

r001.rationale: The response says there is “a lot of biology in between,” but does not identify limited biological understanding as the hardest barrier.

r002.rationale: It does not discuss AlphaFold 3, small-molecule binding prediction, or a capability AlphaFold 2 lacked.

r003.rationale: It separates knowing whether inhibiting a target would help a patient from finding a molecule that changes the target’s function and reaches the right tissue safely.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key distinction is that understanding a protein’s structure and knowing how to intervene in a disease are different problems. A structure can give you an enormously useful starting point, but it doesn’t tell you whether changing that protein’s activity will help a patient, or whether you can make a molecule that does it safely.

There’s also a lot of biology beyond a single structure: how the protein moves, what it interacts with, and which states matter for its function. Then there are all the challenges of the molecule itself—does it bind, does it get to the right tissue, does it have unwanted effects?

So I see AlphaFold as helping scientists ask better questions and move through some parts of that process more quickly. The exciting thing is what people can build on top of it. But the connection to a drug still has to be established through experiments.

r001.rationale: The response mentions biology beyond a single structure, but does not identify limited biological understanding as the hardest barrier to translating structural advances into treatments.

r002.rationale: It does not discuss AlphaFold 3, small-molecule binding prediction, or how that differs from AlphaFold 2.

r003.rationale: It distinguishes knowing whether changing a protein’s activity would help a patient from making a molecule that can carry out that change safely.
